artiest/arthur-collins.text:
Arthur Collins was an American baritone and actor, born in 1864 in Philadelphia and later raised in New Jersey. He had singing lessons, toured for more than fifteen years with theatre companies and appeared in summer opera. Real success came only when, around 1898, he discovered the recording studio. Until his retirement in 1926 he recorded for virtually every record company in the United States. He is thus among the first true recording artists.

Collins specialised in ragtime songs and in the dialect numbers of vaudeville and minstrel shows, a genre that present-day listeners find uncomfortable because of its racist caricature. He used all kinds of vocal effects and character voices, so that it seemed as though more people were standing around the horn. From 1901 he worked with the tenor Joe Natus, later mainly with Byron G. Harlan. In 1909 he joined the Peerless Quartet. His best-known recording is The Preacher and the Bear from 1905, which was the most popular non-operatic recording of the first decade of the century and sold more than a million copies.

Collins was called the king of ragtime singers and recorded more ragtime songs than anyone else of his time. Together with Harlan he made That Funny Jas Band from Dixieland in 1917, the earliest known record on which the word jazz is heard. His recordings let you hear how popular music sounded just before jazz and radio took over.
artiest/arthur-collins.listen: Listen to The Preacher and the Bear. Notice how Collins sets the joke and the storytelling tone with his voice alone, still without a microphone and with a small accompanying group.

artiest/arthur-crudup.text:
Arthur Crudup, nicknamed Big Boy, was an American bluesman from the Mississippi Delta. He was born in 1905 in Forest, Mississippi, into a family of itinerant farm labourers. He first sang gospel and learned guitar from a local bluesman. Around 1940 he moved to Chicago, where he barely scraped a living as a street singer. The producer Lester Melrose discovered him and signed him to Bluebird, a label of RCA Victor.

In the 1940s Crudup recorded songs that became popular in the South, such as Mean Old 'Frisco Blues, So Glad You're Mine, My Baby Left Me and That's All Right of 1946. His music was simple and driving: a rough electric guitar, a powerful voice and a rhythm that pushed forward. Some experts see in That's All Right the first rock 'n' roll song, perhaps even with the first guitar solo.

When Elvis Presley recorded his own version of That's All Right in 1954, Crudup became known as the father of rock 'n' roll. Presley said that he wanted to be as good as Crudup one day. But the money did not reach him. Because of disputes over royalties he stopped recording in the 1950s and worked as a farm labourer. "I was born poor, I live poor and I will die poor," he said in 1970. He died in 1974. His story shows how Black musicians laid the foundations of rock 'n' roll while others got rich from it.
artiest/arthur-crudup.listen: First listen to That's All Right by Arthur Crudup from 1946 and then to the version by Elvis Presley from 1954. Notice what Presley takes over and what he changes: the tempo, the guitar and the way of singing.

artiest/arthur-freed.text:
Arthur Freed was born Arthur Grossman in 1894 in Charleston, South Carolina. He began as a song plugger and pianist in Chicago, sang for a while in the act of the Marx Brothers and then wrote songs. At the film studio Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer he wrote lyrics for films for years, often to music by Nacio Herb Brown. His song I Cried for You, written with Gus Arnheim and Abe Lyman, has become a standard.

In 1939 he worked uncredited on The Wizard of Oz as assistant to the producer. After that he was given his own unit within MGM and turned the studio into the biggest maker of film musicals. His first film as a producer was Babes in Arms, with Mickey Rooney and Judy Garland. Freed brought people from Broadway to Hollywood, among them Vincente Minnelli, Betty Comden, Adolph Green and Roger Edens. He advanced the careers of Gene Kelly, Frank Sinatra and Lena Horne and brought Fred Astaire back for Easter Parade. Singin' in the Rain also came from his production, with songs that he himself had written earlier.

Freed gave his directors and choreographers a great deal of freedom, which was unusual at the time. Thus An American in Paris of 1951 got a fifteen-minute ballet as its finale, and Lerner and Loewe were given complete control over Gigi of 1958. Both films won the Oscar for Best Picture. Freed left MGM in 1961. Without his work the film musical of the 1940s and 1950s would have looked different, and many songs from those films live on in jazz and popular music.
artiest/arthur-freed.listen: Listen to I Cried for You in a recording of your choice. Notice the simple, singable melody and the lyrics that tell a whole story in a few lines.

artiest/arthur-honegger.text: Arthur Honegger was a Swiss, born in Le Havre, who built his career in Paris. He belonged to Les Six, a group of young French composers around 1920. Honegger was one of the first concert composers to write seriously for film. For the director Abel Gance he made the music for La roue (1923) and for the great silent epic Napoléon (1927). His score for Raymond Bernard's Les misérables (1934) is an early example of a full symphonic film score in the sound film. His style is powerful and contrapuntal, with solid brass parts and motoric rhythms. He also wrote for British films, such as Pygmalion (1938).
artiest/arthur-honegger.listen: Listen to the dense, contrapuntal orchestral writing and the heavy brass chords that give the scenes a monumental character.

artiest/arthur-johnston.text:
Arthur Johnston was an American composer, conductor, pianist and arranger. He was born in 1898 in New York, as a boy played piano in cinemas and at sixteen worked for the music publisher Fred Fisher. There he was noticed by Irving Berlin, who took him on as his personal arranger and as conductor of the first Music Box Revues. His first hit was Mandy Make Up Your Mind, written for Florence Mills in the show Dixie to Broadway.

In 1929 Johnston moved to Hollywood. There he orchestrated the music for, among others, Puttin' On the Ritz and Charlie Chaplin's City Lights. With the lyricist Sam Coslow he made songs such as Just One More Chance in 1932 and Cocktails for Two in 1934. After that he became closely associated with Bing Crosby, for whom he wrote in films such as College Humor, Too Much Harmony and Pennies From Heaven. On that last film his collaboration with Johnny Burke began. Together they received an Oscar nomination in 1936 for the title song. Later he also wrote the title song of Song of the South of 1947.

Johnston wrote melodies that lend themselves to both singing and improvisation, and jazz musicians therefore liked to pick them up. Moon Song, My Old Flame and Pennies From Heaven are among the standards of the early American songbook. He was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame and died in 1954 in California.
artiest/arthur-johnston.listen: Listen to Pennies From Heaven in a version of your choice. Notice the simple melody that a jazz musician can easily make his own.

artiest/arthur-rubinstein.text:
Arthur Rubinstein, called Artur in Poland, was a Polish and later American pianist. He was born in 1887 in Łódź, the youngest of seven children. Even as a child he had perfect pitch and at the age of four caught the attention of the violinist Joseph Joachim. At ten he went to Berlin to study, and at thirteen he played for the first time with the Berliner Philharmoniker. In 1904 he settled in Paris, where he met Ravel and Dukas. In 1906 he made his debut at Carnegie Hall.

Rubinstein performed in public for eighty years. He was known as a soloist and as a chamber musician and worked with, among others, Jascha Heifetz, Pablo Casals and Gregor Piatigorsky. During the war years he lived in Los Angeles and in 1946 became an American citizen. For Hollywood he played the piano music in Song of Love. The film Arthur Rubinstein, the Love of Life won an Oscar for best documentary in 1969. He recorded much of the core repertoire, especially the Romantics, and was highly praised as an interpreter of Chopin, of whom he recorded almost everything except the études. He also held Spanish and South American composers such as Albéniz, Falla and Villa-Lobos in high regard. In 1976, at the age of eighty-nine, he gave his farewell concert at Wigmore Hall in London.

His playing was regarded as warm, natural and driven by a zest for life, and he memorised a great deal. Rubinstein showed that classical music could also reach a large audience, and his recordings from the 1940s and 1950s have become, for many listeners, their first introduction to the piano concerto.
artiest/arthur-rubinstein.listen: Listen to a piano concerto played by Rubinstein, for example Tchaikovsky's Piano Concerto No. 1 from 1947. Notice how the piano sings in the quiet passages and how power and softness alternate.

artiest/artie-shaw.text:
Artie Shaw, born Arthur Jacob Arshawsky, was an American clarinettist, composer and bandleader. He was born in 1910 in New York and grew up in New Haven. At thirteen he learned to play the saxophone, at sixteen he switched to clarinet and went on the road with a band. In the 1930s he worked as a studio musician and played in orchestras, until in 1935 he attracted attention with Interlude in B-flat, a piece for rhythm section and string quartet that was later seen as an early example of Third Stream.

His breakthrough came in 1938 with Cole Porter's Begin the Beguine. Hits followed such as Stardust, Back Bay Shuffle, Moonglow and Frenesi. In 1938 he hired Billie Holiday as his singer, the first white bandleader to tour the segregated South with a permanent Black singer. Besides his big orchestra he had a small group, the Gramercy Five, which included a harpsichord, among other instruments. With it he had Summit Ridge Drive. Shaw also added strings to the big band, so that he got more colour and could play ballads. In the Second World War he served in the navy. In 1954 he gave up music altogether and wrote books.

Shaw above all wanted to make music, and hated celebrity life and the endless repetition of the same hits. His bands kept starting and ending again. Even so he is regarded as one of the best clarinettists in jazz, with a fluid, clear tone and an open ear for other styles.
artiest/artie-shaw.listen: Listen to Begin the Beguine from 1938. Notice Shaw's own clarinet and how the orchestra keeps a light, danceable movement around his solo.

artiest/artists-united-against-apartheid.text:
Artists United Against Apartheid was a protest group set up in 1985 by the guitarist and activist Steven Van Zandt and the producer Arthur Baker. The aim was resistance to apartheid in South Africa. The song Sun City was aimed at the luxury resort of that name, with a casino, in Bophuthatswana, a homeland that the South African government had declared independent. Despite an international boycott, well-known Western artists nevertheless performed there. The journalist Danny Schechter suggested making a different kind of We Are the World out of it: a song about change, not about charity.

Van Zandt, Baker and Schechter searched for months for participants. First a few regular backing singers of Baker's recorded the chorus I ain't gonna play Sun City. On top of that came dozens of voices from very different corners: rappers such as Run-DMC, Grandmaster Melle Mel, Kurtis Blow and Afrika Bambaataa, rockers such as Bruce Springsteen, Bob Dylan, Lou Reed, Bono and Peter Gabriel, soul singers such as David Ruffin and Bobby Womack, and jazz musicians such as Miles Davis and Herbie Hancock. All the participants promised never to perform at Sun City.

The result was a raw, stomping track in which rock, hip hop, funk and soul run together. At the same time the album Sun City came into being, along with a documentary about the recording. Sun City shows that the great benefit projects of the 1980s could also be political, and that hip hop and rock together could carry a message.
artiest/artists-united-against-apartheid.listen: Listen to Sun City. Notice how the voices alternate quickly: rappers, rock singers and soul singers each get a few lines. Hear how the chorus I ain't gonna play Sun City is chanted again and again by a choir.

artiest/arvo-part.text: Arvo Pärt, from Estonia, first wrote twelve-tone and collage music, which brought him into conflict with the Soviet regime. After years of silence and study of Gregorian chant and early polyphony he found his own style in 1976, which he called tintinnabuli, after the Latin word for little bells. In it a melody moving in steps sounds together with the notes of a single triad. Spiegel im Spiegel from 1978, for violin and piano, lets you hear that principle in its simplest form.
artiest/arvo-part.listen: Listen to Spiegel im Spiegel and hear how the piano calmly keeps repeating triads, while the violin steps one note further each time and returns again.

artiest/asha-bhosle.text:
Asha Bhosle was born in 1933 as Asha Mangeshkar in Goar near Sangli, in present-day Maharashtra, into a musical family. Her father Deenanath Mangeshkar was an actor and classical singer in Marathi music theatre. Her older sister was the singer Lata Mangeshkar. She called herself an accidental singer who learned by listening to her father, his pupils and her sister. She practised daily, because music was for her the same as breathing. She died in 2026.

Asha Bhosle was a playback singer, someone who sings the songs for actors in films. In the late 1940s and early 1950s the field was dominated by Geeta Dutt, Shamshad Begum and Lata Mangeshkar. In the 1950s she sang more songs than most other female singers, above all in low-budget films. Her work encompassed film music, pop, ghazals, bhajans, Indian classical music, folk songs, qawwalis and Rabindra Sangeet. In a career of more than eighty years she was regarded as one of the most versatile and influential female singers of Hindi film. She named Elvis Presley among her examples.

Her voice is a soprano, agile and versatile. Dum Maro Dum, from the 1971 film Hare Rama Hare Krishna, lets you hear her from a sultry, modern side, in the pop and rock-like music that the composer R. D. Burman wrote for the film. In this way she helped renew the sound of Hindi film in the 1970s.
artiest/asha-bhosle.listen: Listen to Dum Maro Dum and notice the loose, almost whispered way of singing and the rhythmic accompaniment underneath. Hear how her voice glides between the instruments.

artiest/asko-ensemble.text:
The Asko Ensemble was a Dutch ensemble for contemporary classical music, founded in 1965 and based in Amsterdam. For the first five years it was led by Jan Vriend, after which it worked with Cliff Crego, among others, and with conductors such as Riccardo Chailly, Oliver Knussen, Reinbert de Leeuw, George Benjamin, Stefan Asbury and Peter Rundel. In 2009 the ensemble merged with the Schönberg Ensemble to form Asko|Schönberg, which in 2025 took the name Het Muziek.

The ensemble gave regular concerts and also made programmes with film music, dance and multimedia, and performed modern opera. It released almost a hundred recordings, with work by Louis Andriessen, Elliott Carter, György Ligeti, Bruno Maderna, Olivier Messiaen, Edgard Varèse, Claude Vivier and Iannis Xenakis. A series of CDs, the Ligeti Project, was devoted entirely to Ligeti and includes his Hamburg Concerto and Double Concerto, among others. Messiaen's Des canyons aux étoiles also appeared on CD in 1994.

The first performances were important. The Asko Ensemble gave the first performance of Brian Ferneyhough's Terrain in 1992, of parts of Karlheinz Stockhausen's Mittwoch aus Licht in 1996, of Elliott Carter's Asko Concerto in 2000 and of Ligeti's Hamburg Concerto in 2001. Michel van der Aa's opera After Life in 2006 was also first heard here. In this way the ensemble brought new music by living composers to the public and kept the Dutch tradition of modern music alive.
artiest/asko-ensemble.listen: Listen to Ligeti's Hamburg Concerto in the recording by the Asko Ensemble. Notice the unusual tone colours of the instruments and how the ensemble holds the many small motifs together.

artiest/assi-rahbani.text:
Assi Rahbani was a Lebanese composer, musician, conductor and producer. He was born in 1923 and, together with his brother Mansour, formed the Rahbani Brothers. His musical career began at the station Near East Radio. There in 1951 he noticed the singer Nouhad Haddad in the station's choir, who later became known as Fairuz. Assi wrote her very first song, Itab. That began a collaboration among the three that would last almost thirty years.

In 1954 Assi married Fairuz. Together with his brother he wrote not only songs but also musicals for the stage. When the Lebanese civil war broke out, the Rahbanis continued to use political satire and sharp criticism. In 1977 their musical Petra was staged in both the Muslim west and the Christian east of Beirut. In 1978 the trio toured Europe and the Gulf states. In 1972 Assi suffered a brain haemorrhage, and after three operations he recovered. In the late 1970s his health deteriorated. In 1979 the collaboration and the marriage with Fairuz ended. He died in 1986.

With their songs and plays the Rahbani Brothers became a fixture of Lebanese music, and their work remained politically engaged over the years. Their son Ziad Rahbani later became a musician, theatre-maker and political activist himself. Assi's work shows how a national repertoire can arise from radio, theatre and song.
artiest/assi-rahbani.listen: Listen to a song by Fairuz from the 1950s, such as Itab, the first song that Assi wrote for her. Notice her clear voice and the simplicity of the melody.

artiest/astor-piazzolla.text:
Astor Piazzolla was born in 1921 in Mar del Plata in Argentina, the only child of Vicente Piazzolla and Asunta Manetti. In 1925 the family moved to Greenwich Village in New York, a rough neighbourhood, and later to Little Italy. In 1932 he composed his first tango, La Catinga. After returning to Argentina in 1936 he played in tango orchestras, and in 1939 he joined the orchestra of the bandoneon player Aníbal Troilo. His new ideas clashed with Troilo, and in 1944 he left.

Piazzolla studied classical music, with Alberto Ginastera among others, and in 1954 he travelled to Paris to take lessons with Nadia Boulanger. In Paris he also heard the octet of the saxophonist Gerry Mulligan. Back in Argentina he formed an orchestra of strings and the Octeto Buenos Aires, and later his quintet. In 1974 he recorded the album Libertango in Milan, under a contract with an Italian publisher. That same year an album with Gerry Mulligan followed.

His work changed the traditional tango into a new style, nuevo tango, with elements from jazz and classical music. The bandoneon, a kind of concertina, remains the voice, but the rhythms are sharper and the harmonies bolder. Stephen Holden called him in 1992 the most important tango composer in the world. Piazzolla died that year at the age of 71.
artiest/astor-piazzolla.listen: Listen to Libertango and notice the rhythm that keeps driving the tango on and the bandoneon that rises above it. Try to hear where the dance turns into something that is almost rock.

artiest/astrud-gilberto.text:
Astrud Gilberto was a Brazilian singer of bossa nova and samba. She was born in 1940 as Astrud Weinert in Salvador, the daughter of a Brazilian mother and a German father who taught languages. As a result she spoke fluent English. She grew up in Rio de Janeiro and in the late 1950s belonged to the young circle around the emerging bossa nova. In 1960 she married the guitarist and singer João Gilberto, one of the founders of that music. At a festival that year she stood on a stage for the first time, next to her husband.

In 1963 she went with him to New York, as interpreter for João, who spoke no English. There he recorded the album Getz/Gilberto with the saxophonist Stan Getz and the composer Antônio Carlos Jobim. The producer Creed Taylor wanted an English lyric for The Girl from Ipanema. João could not sing in English and Getz did not want to, so Astrud sang it. Her soft, almost whispering voice with a slight accent suited the song perfectly. The album appeared in 1964 and made bossa nova known far beyond the jazz audience. Even so she received only a one-off fee and was not listed among the musicians on the cover.

After the success she went on tour with Getz and continued to live in the United States. She went on to make dozens of albums, such as The Astrud Gilberto Album (1965) and Beach Samba (1967), and was especially popular in Japan as well. Fans called her the queen of bossa nova. In 2002 she stopped singing. She died in 2023.
artiest/astrud-gilberto.listen: Listen to The Girl from Ipanema from 1964. Notice the difference between the Portuguese verse of João Gilberto and the English verse of Astrud, and her calm, almost whispering way of singing.

artiest/atahualpa-yupanqui.text: Atahualpa Yupanqui, born Héctor Roberto Chavero, chose a stage name after two Inca kings. He travelled through the north of Argentina and learned the songs of farmers and indigenous communities. With only guitar and voice he made songs such as Camino del indio and Los ejes de mi carreta. After years of censorship and exile, Édith Piaf invited him to Paris in 1950, and later he lived for a long time in France.
artiest/atahualpa-yupanqui.listen: Listen to Los Ejes de Mi Carreta: a slow guitar, a dark voice and a lyric about a cartwheel creaking along the road.

artiest/atticus-ross.text:
Atticus Ross is an English musician, composer, producer and sound engineer, born in 1968 in Ladbroke Grove in London. In the mid-1990s he made his name as a synthesizer programmer for Tim Simenon's Bomb the Bass, and he worked with Barry Adamson. After that he started a band of his own, 12 Rounds. In 2000 he moved to the United States and from 2002 worked with Trent Reznor on the side project Tapeworm. From 2005 he worked for Nine Inch Nails, first as programmer and producer, and since 2016 as the only official member besides Reznor.

Ross and Reznor became best known for film music. Ross began with it in 2004 with the TV series Touching Evil, followed by The Book of Eli in 2010. For David Fincher's The Social Network they received an Oscar for best original score in 2010. For The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo a Grammy followed, and for Gone Girl in 2014 another collaboration with Fincher. They also wrote the music for Love & Mercy, about Brian Wilson, in 2015, and for Soul they received an Oscar together with Jon Batiste in 2021. In 2020 Ross was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame as a member of Nine Inch Nails.

His work uses electronic sounds, programming and studio technique as an instrument, and comes out of industrial and electronic rock. Ross shows how you can have an influence behind the scenes on the popular music of an entire period: as programmer, producer and composer he turned his studio work into a second career in film.
artiest/atticus-ross.listen: Listen to a piece from the music of The Social Network, for example one of the quiet electronic tracks. Notice how cold, repeated sounds build a tense atmosphere.

artiest/augustus-pablo.text:
Augustus Pablo, really Horace Michael Swaby, was a Jamaican composer, producer and multi-instrumentalist in roots reggae and dub. He was born in 1953 in St. Andrew and learned to play the organ at Kingston College School, where a girl lent him a melodica. That instrument became his trademark. He met Herman Chin Loy, for whose label Aquarius he recorded tracks between 1971 and 1973 such as Higgi Higgi, East of the River Nile and The Red Sea. With Clive Chin he made Java in 1972. Later he founded the labels Hot Stuff, Message and Rockers, named after his brother's sound system.

His album This Is Augustus Pablo appeared in 1974. With Jacob Miller he recorded Baby I Love You So that same year. The dub version, mixed by King Tubby, was released as King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown and appears in Rolling Stone's list of the best tracks of all time. In the 1970s Pablo also produced Fred Locks's Black Star Liner and worked with Dillinger, I-Roy, the Heptones, Bob Marley, Horace Andy and many others. In 1997 he played melodica on the track Star by Primal Scream. He died in 1999 of a collapsed lung, after being ill for a long time.

Pablo was a Rasta and his music has a serious, almost prayerful tone. The melodica sounds hollow and a little sad in his work, above heavy bass lines and spacious dub effects. He showed that the melodica can be a serious solo instrument in reggae. His son Addis Pablo and his daughter Isis Swaby also became musicians.
artiest/augustus-pablo.listen: Listen to King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown. Notice the melodica above the heavy bass and how King Tubby makes sounds surface and disappear in the dub mix.

artiest/augustus-pablo-en-king-tubby.text:
Augustus Pablo, born Horace Swaby in 1953 in St. Andrew in Jamaica, was a composer, producer and multi-instrumentalist in roots reggae and dub. At Kingston College he learned to play the organ and was lent a melodica by a girl, the wind instrument with keys for which he became known. He met the producer Herman Chin Loy and played with the Now Generation, Mikey Chung's band. In 1972 he recorded Java with Clive Chin. He worked with Lee Perry, Bob Marley, Horace Andy and the Heptones, among others.

In 1974 he recorded Baby I Love You So with Jacob Miller. His dub version, King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown, was mixed by the sound engineer King Tubby and appears at number 266 in Rolling Stone's list. In 1976 the album King Tubbys Meets Rockers Uptown appeared. Later albums are East of the River Nile from 1978 and Original Rockers from 1979. In 1997 he played melodica on Star by Primal Scream. Pablo died in 1999 of a collapsed lung, after having suffered for a long time from the nerve disease myasthenia gravis.

Dub is reggae in which the engineer in the studio takes the tracks apart: the bass and the percussion remain, while the vocals and the instruments come and go, with echo and reverb. The melodica therefore sounds like a ghostly, somewhat sad voice. In this way the mixing desk became an instrument and dub grew into an inspiration for later dance and electronic music.
artiest/augustus-pablo-en-king-tubby.listen: Listen to King Tubby Meets Rockers Uptown and notice the melodica and the echo that makes the sound vanish and return. Follow the bass and the percussion, which stay standing while the rest slides in and out of view.

artiest/austin-wintory.text: Austin Wintory (born 1984) studied at the University of Southern California. He became known with the games of thatgamecompany, first flOw (2006) and then Journey (2012). In Journey the player travels through a desert without words. The solo cello is the voice of the player, and the music grows along with the journey, from a quiet beginning to a grand ending. The score was the first game soundtrack to be nominated for a Grammy. For The Banner Saga (2014) Wintory wrote a sober, Nordic-sounding score for wind ensemble and voices. He shows that game music can tell a story without text.
artiest/austin-wintory.listen: Notice the solo cello and how a simple motif returns more and more often and more fully, with more instruments as the journey goes on.

artiest/autechre.text:
Autechre is an English electronic music duo: Rob Brown and Sean Booth from Rochdale near Manchester. They met in 1987 through friends from Manchester's graffiti and breakdancing scene. Shaped by electro, hip hop and acid house, they first swapped cassette mixes and then made their own tracks with cheap equipment, such as a Casio SK-1 sampler and a Roland TR-606 drum machine. Their first single under the name Autechre was Cavity Job in 1991. According to Booth, the name came from keys that they pressed at random on an Atari.

In 1992 they signed with Warp Records and contributed Crystel and The Egg to the compilation Artificial Intelligence. Their debut album Incunabula appeared in 1993, with Eggshell, a reworking of The Egg. In 1994 Amber followed, which critics find more ambient. Tri Repetae from 1995 sounds harder and more mechanical, and Chiastic Slide from 1997 is more about texture than about beats. LP5 from 1998 and Confield from 2001 are also Warp albums. In 1994 they made the Anti EP as a protest against the British law against rave music, which described music as characterised by a succession of repetitive beats.

Their music developed from melodic techno into abstract, experimental music with a complex structure and few stylistic rules. Autechre is regarded as one of the best-known names on Warp and showed that electronic music did not have to be only danceable, but could also be a listening experience.
artiest/autechre.listen: Listen to Crystel and notice the soft, melodic sound of the synthesizers and the rhythm that keeps running underneath. Try to hear how warm that early electronic music sounds compared with their later work.

artiest/avanti-chamber-orchestra.text:
The Avanti! Chamber Orchestra is a Finnish ensemble that focuses on contemporary music. It was founded in 1983 on the initiative of the conductors Esa-Pekka Salonen and Jukka-Pekka Saraste and the flautist Olli Pohjola. The line-up varies from performance to performance, from a single soloist to a whole symphony orchestra. The ensemble is not tied to one genre, but often chooses new music. One example is HumppAvanti!, a collaboration with the musician Timo Hietala in which humppa and other styles come together.

The debut album earned the orchestra the Gramophone Prize of the Finnish broadcaster YLE. Later came recordings with work by Finnish composers, such as the CD Society of Finnish Composers 50th Anniversary from 1995, and records such as Firmamentum from 1997 and From the Grammar of Dreams from 2000. The orchestra often works with Finnish conductors and with international names such as Heinz Holliger, Oliver Knussen, Ralf Gothoni, Gidon Kremer and Charles Neidich. From 1994 to 1998 Anssi Karttunen was artistic director. Since 1998 that has been the clarinettist Kari Kriikku, who was nominated for the Nordic Council Music Prize in 2001.

Since 1986 the orchestra has organised its own festival, Summer Sounds, in Porvoo every summer. Since the late 1990s the festival has invited a different artistic director each year, from Kaija Saariaho and Magnus Lindberg to Barbara Hannigan and Helmut Lachenmann. In this way Avanti! introduces the Finnish public every year to a foreign guest composer, and Finland remains an important country for contemporary classical music.
artiest/avanti-chamber-orchestra.listen: Listen to a recording by Avanti! with work by a Finnish composer, for example from the CD From the Grammar of Dreams. Notice how clearly the small orchestra lets the different instruments sound.

artiest/avicii.text:
Avicii was the stage name of Tim Bergling, a Swedish DJ and producer from Stockholm, where he was born in 1989. At sixteen he began making music with a pirated copy of the program FL Studio and put his remixes on internet forums to get reactions. He took his name from Avīci, the deepest level of hell in Buddhism. He chose it because his real name was already taken on Myspace.

In 2011 he released Levels, which reached the top ten in fifteen countries and was his breakthrough. His music was above all house with a pop feel: big, cheerful synthesizer melodies, a solid four-on-the-floor beat and a chorus that was sung along to in packed halls. On his debut album True (2013) he went further. He mixed house with folk, country and bluegrass, with acoustic guitars and singers such as Aloe Blacc. The single Wake Me Up became one of the most streamed tracks on Spotify. In 2015 Stories followed.

Avicii helped bring electronic dance music, EDM, to the big pop audience and is regarded as one of the most successful DJs ever. Behind the success was a shy young man who struggled with anxiety, alcohol and later painkillers. In 2016 he stopped performing. In 2018 he died in Oman, aged 28. A year later the album Tim was still released.
artiest/avicii.listen: Listen to Levels from 2011. Notice the build-up: how the track slowly builds tension and then bursts into the high, cheerful synthesizer melody that you recognise at once.

artiest/axis-of-awesome.text:
The Axis of Awesome was an Australian trio that combined music and humour. Jordan Raskopoulos, Lee Naimo and Benny Davis began in 2006 in Sydney. They came from the improv theatre of the University of Sydney and were looking for something new. Their name was a pun on the axis of evil, the axis of evil of which the American president George W. Bush spoke. They played at comedy nights, had a regular slot on the radio and broke through with rap parodies of the Australian elections of 2007.

In 2008 they performed at the Melbourne comedy festival and at the Fringe in Edinburgh. After that BBC Radio 1 played their track 4 Chords: a medley of thirty-six pop songs that are all built on the same four chords. The clip went all around the world and was viewed millions of times on YouTube. Albums followed such as Infinity Rock Explosion! (2010) and Viva La Vida Loca Las Vegas (2016). In 2018 the group called it a day.

The trio made both its own songs and parodies of well-known pop songs, in all kinds of styles. 4 Chords became above all a lesson in music theory: it showed in a funny way how often hitmakers use the same chord changes. For that reason the sketch is still used to explain how pop songs are put together.
artiest/axis-of-awesome.listen: Listen to 4 Chords by The Axis of Awesome. Notice how the accompaniment stays the same while the melodies flow from one well-known song into the next. Try to count how many songs you recognise.

artiest/axl-rose.text:
Axl Rose, born William Bruce Rose Jr., is an American singer and songwriter, born in 1962 in Lafayette, Indiana. As a child he sang in the church choir and learned piano at school. In December 1982 he moved to Los Angeles, where he played in bands such as Rapidfire, Hollywood Rose and L.A. Guns. In 1985, with Tracii Guns, he founded Guns N' Roses by merging those bands. The line-up soon consisted of Rose, Slash, Izzy Stradlin, Duff McKagan and Steven Adler. Rose has been the only constant member ever since.

The debut album Appetite for Destruction from 1987 made the band world-famous and contains Sweet Child o' Mine, a song that took the United States to the top of the chart. In 1991 the two albums Use Your Illusion I and II appeared, which entered the American charts high straight away. The tour that followed was full of conflicts and riots. After that Rose was silent for a long time. He returned in 2001 with a new line-up and released Chinese Democracy in 2008. In 2012 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. In 2016 he found Slash and McKagan again for a new tour.

His voice has a wide range and can shoot from a deep, raw tone to a shrill scream. His voice was ranked among the best of all time by Rolling Stone, NME and Billboard. He is therefore regarded as one of the great rock singers of his generation, and his songs still have a place in stadiums.
artiest/axl-rose.listen: Listen to Sweet Child o' Mine from Appetite for Destruction. Notice the wide range of Rose's voice, from low and raw to high and shrill.

artiest/b-j-thomas.text:
B.J. Thomas, in full Billy Joe Thomas, was an American singer who became known with country, pop and Christian music. He was born in 1942 in Hugo, Oklahoma, grew up near Houston and sang in a church choir as a teenager. After that he became the singer of The Triumphs. In 1966 the album I'm So Lonesome I Could Cry appeared, with a cover of the Hank Williams song, which sold more than a million copies and earned a gold record.

His breakthrough in pop came in 1968 with Hooked on a Feeling. In 1969 he sang in the film Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid the song Raindrops Keep Fallin' on My Head by Burt Bacharach and Hal David. It won an Oscar for best film song and in January 1970 reached the top of the Billboard Hot 100. In 1972 he left Scepter Records. In 1975 he had another number one with (Hey Won't You Play) Another Somebody Done Somebody Wrong Song, the song with the longest title ever to reach that position. His last hit in the American top forty was Don't Worry Baby from 1977. In 2014 Raindrops Keep Fallin' on My Head was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame. He died in 2021.

Thomas had a warm, relaxed voice that suited light, melodic pop and country. His work shows how pop of the 1960s and 1970s with a Bacharach melody could go together with a soft southern tone.
artiest/b-j-thomas.listen: Listen to Raindrops Keep Fallin' on My Head. Notice how light and almost casual Thomas sings, above a melody that skips along cheerfully.

artiest/baauer.text:
Baauer is the stage name of Harry Bauer Rodrigues, an American producer and DJ, born in 1989 in Philadelphia. He grew up in Germany, London and Connecticut and was already making dance music at the age of thirteen. Earlier he released a track under the name Captain Harry, which was supported by BBC Radio 1. Around 2012 his first releases belonged to an emerging movement in electronic music, trap, alongside TNGHT, RL Grime, Rustie and Flosstradamus.

His first official single Harlem Shake came out in May 2012 free on SoundCloud, on Mad Decent's label Jeffrees. Rustie first played the track in a mix for BBC Radio 1. Later it became a viral video craze on YouTube, when thousands of fans, artists and brands made their own dance videos. After a rule change by Billboard in 2013, Harlem Shake became the first number one in the United States to chart purely through streaming. His first EP Dum Dum came out in 2012, followed by ß in 2014. In 2016 the debut album Aa appeared. The second album Planet's Mad from 2020 received a Grammy nomination for best dance or electronic album.

Baauer also produced for Just Blaze, Pusha T, Tom Morello and G-Dragon and made remixes for Missy Elliott, Disclosure and Gorillaz, among others. His music is heard in films such as Logan and Red Sparrow. With Harlem Shake he showed that a piece of electronic music can spread faster through internet culture than through radio.
artiest/baauer.listen: Listen to Harlem Shake. Notice the heavy bass and the hard, jolting rhythms, and how little is needed to make a track stick in the mind.

artiest/babatunde-olatunji.text:
Babatunde Olatunji was born in 1927 in the village of Ajido near Badagry in the Nigerian state of Lagos, a member of the Ogu people. His name means father has returned, because he was born two months after the death of his father. He was being groomed to become a chief, but at the age of twelve decided that he did not want that. Through a scholarship from the Rotary Foundation he came to the United States, to Morehouse College. There he worked with Wendell Whalum on Betelehemu, a Nigerian Christmas song that is still sung by choirs today. At New York University he started a small percussion ensemble to earn some extra money.

Columbia Records signed him in 1958. A year later his first record appeared, Drums of Passion, which was a great success and is still available. Many Americans first encountered world music through it. Later albums included Zungo!, Flaming Drums! and High Life!. He linked Nigerian rhythms with Ghanaian and Afro-Caribbean influences and found an audience among jazz musicians. With the support of John Coltrane he founded the Olatunji Center for African Culture in Harlem, where Coltrane performed for the last time in 1967. Coltrane dedicated the piece Tunji to him. In 1969 Carlos Santana had a hit with Jin-go-lo-ba, under the title Jingo.

Olatunji played with many jazz musicians, including Cannonball Adderley and Max Roach. His music consists of drums, choral singing and call and response, and showed that African rhythms could enrich American popular music. He died in 2003.
artiest/babatunde-olatunji.listen: Listen to Jin-Go-Lo-Ba and notice the drums and the choir's answer to the lead singer. Can you hear how the rhythm seems to get faster and faster while the tempo stays the same?

artiest/baby-dodds.text:
Warren Baby Dodds was an American jazz drummer, born in 1898 in New Orleans. He was the younger brother of the clarinettist Johnny Dodds and came from a musical family: his father and uncle played the violin and his sister the harmonica. His mother died when he was nine. In New Orleans he made a name at an early age as the best young drummer. In 1918 he left Sonny Celestin's group for the riverboat band of Fate Marable, in which the teenage Louis Armstrong also played. In summer the band sailed from New Orleans to St. Louis and sometimes further north, and played jazz, popular and classical music.

In the 1930s Dodds played with Lil Hardin, Natty Dominique and the house band of the Three Deuces. Together with his brother he was heard in King Oliver's band and then in Chicago, where Johnny led his own group. Johnny died in 1940. Baby Dodds suffered a first stroke in 1949 and two more later. He still taught and played as much as he could, but no longer finished all his performances. He recorded the album Talking and Drum Solos in 1951, on which he also talks about his work, and retired in 1957. He died in 1959 in Chicago.

Dodds is regarded as one of the best jazz drummers of the time before the big bands. He mostly kept time with the bass drum and played buzz rolls on the snare on top of it, and he gave his patterns colour with accents and embellishments. His way of playing showed that in early jazz a drummer does not merely keep the tempo, but also has a voice of his own in the collective.
artiest/baby-dodds.listen: Listen to Talking and Drum Solos from 1951. Notice the bass drum keeping the pulse and the rolls on the snare on top of it.

artiest/backstreet-boys.text:
The Backstreet Boys were put together in 1993 in Orlando, Florida: Nick Carter, Howie Dorough, AJ McLean and the cousins Brian Littrell and Kevin Richardson. They were a vocal group, not a band that played instruments itself. With Take That and *NSYNC they belong to the cast boy bands of the 1990s. According to Billboard they are the best-selling boy band ever.

Their first single, We've Got It Goin' On, did little in America, but reached the top five in several European countries. The debut album Backstreet Boys (1996) made the group popular first in Europe, especially in Germany, and only afterwards in its home country. Many of their hits came from Cheiron Studio in Stockholm, where Max Martin and his colleagues made the music and the singers dropped by to sing their parts. I Want It That Way, written by Max Martin and Andreas Carlsson, was recorded there in November 1998. It became the first single from Millennium (1999), which sold about 1.13 million copies in America in its first week. In England I Want It That Way became their only number 1 hit.

In 2006 Richardson left; in 2012 he returned. The group kept performing, with concert residencies in Las Vegas, and in 2013 received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. The Backstreet Boys show how the hit factory worked in the late 1990s: American singers, Swedish songs, and an audience of teenagers who bought albums by the million at a time.
artiest/backstreet-boys.listen: I Want It That Way opens with an acoustic guitar playing a chord in separate notes (an arpeggio); Carlsson said that Metallica's Nothing Else Matters was the inspiration. Listen to how that guitar pattern returns in the verses and how, in the chorus, the voices come to lie on top of one another in harmony.

artiest/bad-brains.text:
Bad Brains is an American punk band from Washington, D.C., founded in 1976. They are seen as pioneers of hardcore punk, although the members resist that term. The group began as a jazz fusion band under the name Mind Power, modelled on Return to Forever and Mahavishnu Orchestra. The line-up consisted of the guitarist Dr. Know, the bassist Darryl Jenifer and the brothers Paul Hudson, later known as H.R., and the drummer Earl Hudson. In 1977 the singer Sid McCray introduced them to punk. They changed their name to Bad Brains, after a song by the Ramones, and after a Bob Marley concert they also became interested in reggae and Rastafari.

The energetic performances won them an audience in Washington, but in 1979 many clubs banned them because of their destructive fans. Banned in D.C. is about that. Around 1980 they moved to New York, where they helped get the hardcore scene going, and in 1982 they played regularly at CBGB. Their debut album Bad Brains appeared in 1982 on the label ROIR, at first on cassette only. Rock for Light followed in 1983 and I Against I in 1986, with influences from heavy metal and funk. Quickness appeared in 1989 and Rise in 1993. The band broke up several times and got back together.

Their music is fast and sharp, with reggae as a place of rest in between. Bands such as Living Colour and Fishbone, who later had success, were influenced by them. Bad Brains shows that punk and reggae together can form a single sound.
artiest/bad-brains.listen: Listen to Banned in D.C. and notice the furious tempo of the guitar and the rhythm, and the sharp voice of the singer. Try to hear how tightly the band plays despite the speed.

artiest/bad-bunny.text:
Bad Bunny is the stage name of Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio, born in 1994 in Bayamón and raised in Vega Baja in Puerto Rico. His father was a lorry driver and his mother a teacher. At home he heard salsa, merengue and pop ballads. At the age of five he was given a record by Vico C, a pioneer of reggaeton. After secondary school he studied audiovisual communication in Arecibo, with the aim of becoming a radio presenter, and worked as a bagger in a supermarket. He did not finish his studies.

In 2016 he broke through with Diles, which earned him a contract with Hear This Music. He became known worldwide with I Like It, a number one in the American Billboard Hot 100. His debut album X 100pre from 2018 appears in Rolling Stone's list of the five hundred best albums. In 2020 YHLQMDLG appeared, and in 2022 Un verano sin ti. He was repeatedly the most streamed artist on Spotify and in 2026 he performed at the Super Bowl halftime show. Outside music he does wrestling and has acted in films.

Bad Bunny is called the King of Latin Trap. He combines trap, reggaeton and other styles with Spanish-language lyrics and has done much to bring Spanish-language rap and pop to the worldwide mainstream. In this way he showed that an artist from Puerto Rico did not have to ask the audience to sing in English.
artiest/bad-bunny.listen: Listen to Estamos Bien and notice the relaxed tempo and the light, almost sung delivery. Try to hear where the rap turns into melody.

artiest/badfinger.text:
Badfinger was a British rock band, formed in 1961 in Swansea in Wales. The best-known line-up consisted of the Welshmen Pete Ham (rhythm guitar and vocals) and Mike Gibbins (drums) and the Englishmen Tom Evans (bass) and Joey Molland (guitar). The group was first called the Iveys, after a street in Swansea, and changed its name to Badfinger, after the working title Bad Finger Boogie of the Beatles song With a Little Help from My Friends from 1967. They played covers of Motown, blues, soul and Beatles in London and in 1967 made demos with Ray Davies of the Kinks.

From 1970 to 1972 Badfinger had four consecutive worldwide hits: Come and Get It, written and produced by Paul McCartney, No Matter What, Day After Day, produced by George Harrison, and Baby Blue, produced by Todd Rundgren. Their song Without You from 1970 was recorded many times and became a number one in Harry Nilsson's version of 1972. Their albums appeared on Apple Records, including Magic Christian Music, No Dice and Straight Up.

After Apple Records ceased to exist in 1973, the group faced legal and financial problems, mainly through fraud by the manager Stan Polley. In 1975 Pete Ham took his own life. Baby Blue was later heard in the final episode of the television series Breaking Bad, through which a new generation discovered the song. The band played clear guitar pop with three voices in harmony, and shows how the Beatles helped the groups around them and sometimes also crushed them.
artiest/badfinger.listen: Listen to No Matter What and notice the solid guitar riff and the harmony singing in the chorus. Try to hear how the harmonies carry the melody.

artiest/bahram-mansurov.text:
Bahram Mansurov was born in 1911 in Baku, into a prosperous family. His father, Meshadi Suleyman bey Mansurov, was known as a philanthropist and great connoisseur of mugham and was a virtuoso on the tar. He often held musical gatherings, majlises, in his house in the old city. Bahram finished school in 1925 and in 1929 was invited to join an orchestra as a tar player. He became a Soviet and Azerbaijani tar player, the lute with two bodies and metal strings that is the most important instrument of mugham in Azerbaijan.

During the war he performed for soldiers and the wounded, and in 1944 he toured several cities in Iran. After the war he received honours. In 1971 and 1975 two records appeared under the auspices of UNESCO, and he took part in international symposia and concerts in Europe. In 1978 he became People's Artist of the Azerbaijan SSR. He donated archive material from the family to museums and archives in the Soviet Union, which is important for the music history of Azerbaijan. Albums by him are Azerbaijani Mugam from 1975 and a record from 1974. He died in 1985 in Baku.

Mansurov helped make mugham, the classical music of Azerbaijan, known outside the country. His playing is an example of the tradition, in which a soloist on the tar builds a long piece on a single mode.
artiest/bahram-mansurov.listen: Listen to Mugam Chahargah and notice the tar that opens the piece and slowly builds it up. Try to hear how the melody keeps returning to the same note.

artiest/baltimora.text:
Baltimora was an Italian music project from Milan, active from 1984 to 1987. The group is best known for the single Tarzan Boy from 1985. In the United Kingdom and the United States it is regarded as a one-hit wonder. Elsewhere in Europe, including Italy, Baltimora had another hit that same year with Woody Boogie.

In 1984 Maurizio Bassi, a producer and musician from Milan, met Jimmy McShane from Derry in Northern Ireland. McShane was a singer, dancer and actor and had tried without success to break through in the theatre in the West End. Together they devised an act with McShane as the face. Bassi hired Italian session musicians for the first album, such as the guitarist Giorgio Cocilovo and the drummer Lele Melotti. Most of the writing was by Bassi and the American lyricist Naimy Hackett. The producer Tom Hooker claims that Bassi recorded the vocals and that McShane sometimes sang along.

Tarzan Boy appeared in April 1985 and became a great European success, with a sixth place in Italy and a place in the top five of several countries. In the United Kingdom the track reached number three in August 1985. In the United States it reached number 13 in the Hot 100 in February 1986. The album Living in the Background appeared at the end of 1985. Survivor in Love from 1987 and the single Key Key Karimba had less success, after which Bassi decided to disband the group. McShane died in 1995 of the consequences of AIDS.

The music belongs to Italo disco: dance music with synthesizers, a tight rhythm and a simple, catchy melody.
artiest/baltimora.listen: Listen to Tarzan Boy and notice the synthesizer riff and the call in the chorus. Try to hear how few notes the song needs.

artiest/bananarama.text:
Bananarama is an English pop group, founded in 1980 in London by three friends: Sara Dallin, Keren Woodward and Siobhan Fahey. The group is important above all as the face of the British hit factory of the 1980s. In 1988 Bananarama entered the Guinness Book of World Records as the girl group with the most entries in the English charts.

The first big hit came in 1982 with It Ain't What You Do (It's the Way That You Do It), together with Fun Boy Three. Cruel Summer (1983) and Robert De Niro's Waiting... (1984) followed. Cruel Summer became a hit in America when it was heard in the film The Karate Kid in 1984. In 1986 they recorded Venus, the song by the Dutch band Shocking Blue, with the producer trio Stock Aitken Waterman. At Fahey's suggestion the producers reworked a first version, which stayed close to the original, into Hi-NRG, in the style of You Spin Me Round by Dead or Alive. Venus became a number 1 in the United States. The album Wow! (1987), with I Heard a Rumour and Love in the First Degree, was written and made by the group entirely together with SAW.

Venus showed that SAW could give an existing song and an existing group a new sound. Shortly afterwards Rick Astley and Kylie Minogue walked into the same studio. Fahey left the group in 1988 and with Marcella Detroit formed the duo Shakespears Sister. Dallin and Woodward carried on as a duo; in 2017 Fahey once again stood on stage with them.
artiest/bananarama.listen: In Venus (1986) the rock band of Shocking Blue has been replaced by a programmed drum machine (a Linn 9000) and synthesizers. Put it next to the original from 1969: the melody is the same, but the song has become a dance record.

artiest/band-aid.text:
Band Aid was a one-off group of British and Irish pop stars who in November 1984 recorded the charity song Do They Know It's Christmas? in a single day. The occasion was a series of BBC reports by the journalist Michael Buerk on the famine in Ethiopia. Bob Geldof, singer of The Boomtown Rats, was deeply affected by them. He phoned Midge Ure of Ultravox, and together they decided to make a record whose proceeds would go to Ethiopia.

Ure wrote a melody on a portable keyboard, and Geldof added lyrics from a song of his own that was half finished. Ure produced the track and made the backing at home with keyboards and drum machines; for the intro he used a sample of the drums from The Hurting by Tears for Fears. Trevor Horn made his London studio available free for a day and a night. On 25 November, among others, Paul Young, Boy George, George Michael, Bono, Sting, Simon Le Bon, Spandau Ballet, Status Quo and Kool & the Gang came there to sing. The verses are divided among individual singers, and everyone sings the chorus together.

The single was released on 7 December 1984 and spent five weeks at number 1 in England, through to Christmas. Within a year it raised eight million pounds. The success led to We Are the World in America and to the Live Aid concert of 1985. There was also criticism: according to some, the lyrics gave a one-sided and condescending picture of Africa. The song was later re-recorded three more times, in 1989, 2004 and 2014.
artiest/band-aid.listen: Listen to Do They Know It's Christmas? from 1984. Notice the echoing drums at the beginning and count how many different voices you hear in the verses. Hear how, in the ending, all the singers keep repeating the same chorus together.

artiest/band-aid-ii.text:
Band Aid II was a second version of the British charity group Band Aid, which in 1989 recorded the song Do They Know It's Christmas? again. The original had been written in 1984 by Bob Geldof and Midge Ure to raise money for the famine in Ethiopia. Geldof had been moved by reports by the BBC journalist Michael Buerk. The first Band Aid, a supergroup of popular British and Irish musicians, recorded the song in a single day in November 1984 at Sarm West Studios in London, with Trevor Horn hosting the studios.

The original came out on 7 December 1984, went straight to number one in the United Kingdom and stayed there for five weeks. It was one of the best-selling singles of its time and within a year raised eight million pounds for Ethiopia. The success inspired We Are the World by USA for Africa and the Live Aid concert in 1985. In 1989 the re-recording followed with other musicians, in the line-up referred to as Band Aid II. Kylie Minogue sang the first line in that version. This version too reached first place in the United Kingdom and became a Christmas number one. Later versions followed in 2004 and 2014.

The song is built from a verse and a bridge, in which individual singers can each sing a line, and a chorus that the whole ensemble repeats. As a result it lends itself well to changing line-ups. Band Aid II showed that the idea of a charity single with famous names still worked after the first wave, although the song also drew criticism for its lyrics.
artiest/band-aid-ii.listen: Listen to Do They Know It's Christmas? in the 1989 version. Notice how each singer gets a line of his or her own and how the whole ensemble sings together in the chorus.
